claim: Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase (APRT) and hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) are two structurally related enzymes involved in purine recycling in humans.
source: Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase (APRT) and hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) are two structurally related enzymes involved in purine recycling in humans.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about these enzymes and their function in human purine metabolism.

claim: Inherited mutations that suppress HGPRT activity are associated with Lesch–Nyhan disease (LND), a rare X-linked metabolic and neurological disorder in children.
source: Inherited mutations that suppress HGPRT activity are associated with Lesch–Nyhan disease (LND), a rare X-linked metabolic and neurological disorder in children, characterized by hyperuricemia, dystonia, and compulsive self-injury.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the genetic basis and characteristics of Lesch-Nyhan disease.

claim: LND is characterized by hyperuricemia, dystonia, and compulsive self-injury.
source: Inherited mutations that suppress HGPRT activity are associated with Lesch–Nyhan disease (LND), a rare X-linked metabolic and neurological disorder in children, characterized by hyperuricemia, dystonia, and compulsive self-injury.
evidence: This describes the clinical symptoms of LND based on established medical knowledge.

claim: No treatment is available for the neurological defects of LND.
source: To date, no treatment is available for these neurological defects and no animal model recapitulates all symptoms of LND patients.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of medical treatment for LND.

claim: No animal model recapitulates all symptoms of LND patients.
source: To date, no treatment is available for these neurological defects and no animal model recapitulates all symptoms of LND patients.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of existing animal models for LND research.

claim: No HGPRT activity is expressed in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: By combining enzymatic assays and phylogenetic analysis, we confirm that no HGPRT activity is expressed in Drosophila melanogaster, making the APRT homolog (Aprt) the only purine-recycling enzyme in this organism.
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic assays and phylogenetic analysis performed in the study.

claim: Aprt is the only purine-recycling enzyme in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: By combining enzymatic assays and phylogenetic analysis, we confirm that no HGPRT activity is expressed in Drosophila melanogaster, making the APRT homolog (Aprt) the only purine-recycling enzyme in this organism.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of HGPRT activity and the presence of Aprt.

claim: APRT deficiency does not trigger neurological defects in humans.
source: Whereas APRT deficiency does not trigger neurological defects in humans, we observed that Drosophila Aprt mutants show both metabolic and neurobehavioral disturbances, including increased uric acid levels, locomotor impairments, sleep alterations, seizure-like behavior, reduced lifespan, and reduction of adenosine signaling and content.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the clinical consequences of APRT deficiency in humans.

claim: Drosophila Aprt mutants show increased uric acid levels.
source: Whereas APRT deficiency does not trigger neurological defects in humans, we observed that Drosophila Aprt mutants show both metabolic and neurobehavioral disturbances, including increased uric acid levels, locomotor impairments, sleep alterations, seizure-like behavior, reduced lifespan, and reduction of adenosine signaling and content.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC measurements of uric acid levels in Aprt mutant flies.

claim: Drosophila Aprt mutants show locomotor impairments.
source: Whereas APRT deficiency does not trigger neurological defects in humans, we observed that Drosophila Aprt mutants show both metabolic and neurobehavioral disturbances, including increased uric acid levels, locomotor impairments, sleep alterations, seizure-like behavior, reduced lifespan, and reduction of adenosine signaling and content.
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data showing reduced climbing performance.

claim: Drosophila Aprt mutants show sleep alterations.
source: Whereas APRT deficiency does not trigger neurological defects in humans, we observed that Drosophila Aprt mutants show both metabolic and neurobehavioral disturbances, including increased uric acid levels, locomotor impairments, sleep alterations, seizure-like behavior, reduced lifespan, and reduction of adenosine signaling and content.
evidence: This is supported by sleep monitoring data showing reduced sleep duration and bout length.

claim: Drosophila Aprt mutants show seizure-like behavior.
source: Whereas APRT deficiency does not trigger neurological defects in humans, we observed that Drosophila Aprt mutants show both metabolic and neurobehavioral disturbances, including increased uric acid levels, locomotor impairments, sleep alterations, seizure-like behavior, reduced lifespan, and reduction of adenosine signaling and content.
evidence: This is supported by bang sensitivity assay data showing prolonged recovery times.

claim: Drosophila Aprt mutants show reduced lifespan.
source: Whereas APRT deficiency does not trigger neurological defects in humans, we observed that Drosophila Aprt mutants show both metabolic and neurobehavioral disturbances, including increased uric acid levels, locomotor impairments, sleep alterations, seizure-like behavior, reduced lifespan, and reduction of adenosine signaling and content.
evidence: This is supported by longevity assay data showing median lifespan of 38 days vs 50 days for wild-type.

claim: Drosophila Aprt mutants show reduction of adenosine signaling and content.
source: Whereas APRT deficiency does not trigger neurological defects in humans, we observed that Drosophila Aprt mutants show both metabolic and neurobehavioral disturbances, including increased uric acid levels, locomotor impairments, sleep alterations, seizure-like behavior, reduced lifespan, and reduction of adenosine signaling and content.
evidence: This is supported by UPLC measurements showing reduced adenosine levels and increased Ent2 expression.

claim: Locomotor defects in Aprt mutants could be rescued by Aprt re-expression in neurons.
source: Locomotor defects could be rescued by Aprt re-expression in neurons and reproduced by knocking down Aprt selectively in the protocerebral anterior medial (PAM) dopaminergic neurons, the mushroom bodies, or glia subsets.
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data showing partial rescue when Aprt is re-expressed in neurons.

claim: Locomotor defects in Aprt mutants could be reproduced by knocking down Aprt selectively in the PAM dopaminergic neurons.
source: Locomotor defects could be rescued by Aprt re-expression in neurons and reproduced by knocking down Aprt selectively in the protocerebral anterior medial (PAM) dopaminergic neurons, the mushroom bodies, or glia subsets.
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data showing locomotor defects when Aprt is knocked down in PAM neurons.

claim: Locomotor defects in Aprt mutants could be reproduced by knocking down Aprt selectively in the mushroom bodies.
source: Locomotor defects could be rescued by Aprt re-expression in neurons and reproduced by knocking down Aprt selectively in the protocerebral anterior medial (PAM) dopaminergic neurons, the mushroom bodies, or glia subsets.
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data showing locomotor defects when Aprt is knocked down in mushroom body neurons.

claim: Locomotor defects in Aprt mutants could be reproduced by knocking down Aprt selectively in glia subsets.
source: Locomotor defects could be rescued by Aprt re-expression in neurons and reproduced by knocking down Aprt selectively in the protocerebral anterior medial (PAM) dopaminergic neurons, the mushroom bodies, or glia subsets.
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data showing locomotor defects when Aprt is knocked down in glial cells.

claim: Ingestion of allopurinol rescued uric acid levels in Aprt-deficient mutants but not neurological defects.
source: Ingestion of allopurinol rescued uric acid levels in Aprt-deficient mutants but not neurological defects, as is the case in LND patients, while feeding adenosine or N6-methyladenosine (m6A) during development fully rescued the epileptic behavior.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data showing normalized uric acid levels and behavioral assays showing no improvement in SING or bang sensitivity.

claim: Allopurinol does not rescue neurological defects in LND patients.
source: Ingestion of allopurinol rescued uric acid levels in Aprt-deficient mutants but not neurological defects, as is the case in LND patients, while feeding adenosine or N6-methyladenosine (m6A) during development fully rescued the epileptic behavior.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the limitations of allopurinol treatment in LND.

claim: Feeding adenosine during development fully rescued the epileptic behavior in Aprt mutants.
source: Ingestion of allopurinol rescued uric acid levels in Aprt-deficient mutants but not neurological defects, as is the case in LND patients, while feeding adenosine or N6-methyladenosine (m6A) during development fully rescued the epileptic behavior.
evidence: This is supported by bang sensitivity assay data showing normalized recovery times after adenosine feeding.

claim: Feeding N6-methyladenosine (m6A) during development fully rescued the epileptic behavior in Aprt mutants.
source: Ingestion of allopurinol rescued uric acid levels in Aprt-deficient mutants but not neurological defects, as is the case in LND patients, while feeding adenosine or N6-methyladenosine (m6A) during development fully rescued the epileptic behavior.
evidence: This is supported by bang sensitivity assay data showing normalized recovery times after m6A feeding.

claim: Pan-neuronal expression of an LND-associated mutant form of human HGPRT (I42T) resulted in early locomotor defects in flies.
source: Intriguingly, pan-neuronal expression of an LND-associated mutant form of human HGPRT (I42T), but not the wild-type enzyme, resulted in early locomotor defects and seizure in flies, similar to Aprt deficiency.
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data showing reduced climbing performance in flies expressing HGPRT-I42T.

claim: Pan-neuronal expression of an LND-associated mutant form of human HGPRT (I42T) resulted in seizure in flies.
source: Intriguingly, pan-neuronal expression of an LND-associated mutant form of human HGPRT (I42T), but not the wild-type enzyme, resulted in early locomotor defects and seizure in flies, similar to Aprt deficiency.
evidence: This is supported by bang sensitivity assay data showing prolonged recovery times in flies expressing HGPRT-I42T.

claim: Pan-neuronal expression of wild-type human HGPRT did not result in locomotor defects or seizure in flies.
source: Intriguingly, pan-neuronal expression of an LND-associated mutant form of human HGPRT (I42T), but not the wild-type enzyme, resulted in early locomotor defects and seizure in flies, similar to Aprt deficiency.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assay data showing no defects in flies expressing wild-type HGPRT.

claim: The purine salvage pathway is an essential component of cellular metabolism that allows the recovery of free purine bases.
source: The purine salvage pathway is an essential component of cellular metabolism that allows the recovery of free purine bases derived from the diet or from the degradation of nucleic acids and nucleotides, thus avoiding the energy cost of de novo purine biosynthesis (Nyhan, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about purine metabolism, supported by citation.

claim: Energy-intensive tissues, such as cardiac muscle and brain cells, extensively use the purine salvage pathway to maintain their purine levels.
source: Energy-intensive tissues, such as cardiac muscle and brain cells, extensively use this pathway to maintain their purine levels (Ipata, 2011; Johnson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about tissue-specific purine metabolism, supported by citations.

claim: HGPRT converts hypoxanthine and guanine into IMP and GMP, respectively.
source: The two main recycling enzymes involved in the salvage pathway in mammals are hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT), which converts hypoxanthine and guanine into IMP and GMP, respectively, and adenine phosphoribosyltransferase (APRT), which converts adenine into AMP.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the enzymatic function of HGPRT.

claim: APRT converts adenine into AMP.
source: The two main recycling enzymes involved in the salvage pathway in mammals are hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT), which converts hypoxanthine and guanine into IMP and GMP, respectively, and adenine phosphoribosyltransferase (APRT), which converts adenine into AMP.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the enzymatic function of APRT.

claim: Loss of APRT leads to the formation of 2,8-dihydroxyadenine crystals in kidney.
source: Loss of APRT seems to have only metabolic consequences, leading to the formation of 2,8-dihydroxyadenine crystals in kidney, which can be fatal but is readily prevented by allopurinol treatment (Bollée et al., 2012; Harambat et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about APRT deficiency in humans, supported by citations.

claim: 2,8-dihydroxyadenine crystal formation in kidney due to APRT loss can be prevented by allopurinol treatment.
source: Loss of APRT seems to have only metabolic consequences, leading to the formation of 2,8-dihydroxyadenine crystals in kidney, which can be fatal but is readily prevented by allopurinol treatment (Bollée et al., 2012; Harambat et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about treatment of APRT deficiency, supported by citations.

claim: Highly inactivating mutations in HGPRT trigger Lesch–Nyhan disease (LND).
source: In contrast, highly inactivating mutations in HGPRT trigger Lesch–Nyhan disease (LND), a rare neurometabolic X-linked recessive disorder with dramatic consequences for child neurodevelopment (Lesch and Nyhan, 1964; Seegmiller et al., 1967).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the genetic basis of LND, supported by citations.

claim: The metabolic consequence of HGPRT deficiency is an overproduction of uric acid in the blood (hyperuricemia).
source: The metabolic consequence of HGPRT deficiency is an overproduction of uric acid in the blood (hyperuricemia) that can lead to gout and tophi, or nephrolithiasis (Sass et al., 1965; Kelley et al., 1967).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the metabolic effects of HGPRT deficiency, supported by citations.

claim: LND patients develop severe neurological impairments, such as dystonia, choreoathetosis, spasticity, and compulsive self-injurious behavior.
source: Affected children also develop severe neurological impairments, such as dystonia, choreoathetosis, spasticity, and a dramatic compulsive self-injurious behavior (Nyhan, 1997; Jinnah et al., 2006; Torres et al., 2007a; Schretlen et al., 2005; Madeo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the neurological symptoms of LND, supported by citations.

claim: LND patients have a developmental delay from 3 to 6 months after birth.
source: They have a developmental delay from 3 to 6 months after birth, and most of them never walk or even sit without support.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the developmental trajectory of LND patients.

claim: Most LND patients never walk or even sit without support.
source: They have a developmental delay from 3 to 6 months after birth, and most of them never walk or even sit without support.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the motor impairments in LND patients.

claim: Xanthine oxidase inhibitors, such as febuxostat or allopurinol, are given to LND patients to decrease their uric acid levels.
source: Xanthine oxidase inhibitors, such as febuxostat or allopurinol, are given to patients after diagnosis to decrease their uric acid levels and prevent the formation of urate crystals in kidney, which can lead to renal failure (Kelley et al., 1967; Torres et al., 2007a; Lahaye et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the treatment of metabolic symptoms in LND, supported by citations.

claim: There is no treatment to alleviate the neurological symptoms of LND.
source: However, there is as yet no treatment to alleviate the neurological symptoms of LND (Torres and Puig, 2007b; Jinnah et al., 2010; Madeo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the limitations of current LND treatments, supported by citations.

claim: The causes of neurobehavioral troubles in LND are still not elucidated.
source: To date, the causes of neurobehavioral troubles in LND are still not elucidated (Jinnah et al., 2010; Bell et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge regarding LND pathogenesis, supported by citations.

claim: The most favored hypothesis for LND neurobehavioral troubles is a dysfunction of the brain's basal ganglia, particularly its dopaminergic pathways.
source: The most favored hypothesis is a dysfunction of the brain's basal ganglia, and particularly of its dopaminergic pathways (Baumeister and Frye, 1985; Visser et al., 2000; Nyhan, 2000; Saito and Takashima, 2000; Egami et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about LND pathogenesis supported by multiple citations.

claim: Analyses revealed a marked loss of dopamine (DA) in the basal ganglia of LND patients.
source: Indeed, analyses revealed a marked loss of dopamine (DA) (Lloyd et al., 1981; Ernst et al., 1996) and DA transporters (Wong et al., 1996) in the basal ganglia of LND patients.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dopamine deficits in LND, supported by citations.

claim: Analyses revealed a marked loss of DA transporters in the basal ganglia of LND patients.
source: Indeed, analyses revealed a marked loss of dopamine (DA) (Lloyd et al., 1981; Ernst et al., 1996) and DA transporters (Wong et al., 1996) in the basal ganglia of LND patients.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dopamine transporter deficits in LND, supported by citation.

claim: DA deficits have been reported in HGPRT knockout rodents, but without motor or behavioral defects.
source: DA deficits have also been reported in HGPRT knockout rodents, but without motor or behavioral defects (Finger et al., 1988; Dunnett et al., 1989; Jinnah et al., 1993; Jinnah et al., 1994; Meek et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about rodent models of LND, supported by citations.

claim: HGPRT deficiency disrupts proliferation and migration of developing midbrain DA neurons in mouse embryos.
source: Recent studies reported that HGPRT deficiency disrupts proliferation and migration of developing midbrain DA neurons in mouse embryos, arguing for a neurodevelopmental syndrome (Witteveen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is recent research finding supported by citation.

claim: HGPRT deficiency could result from ATP depletion and impaired energy metabolism.
source: This could result from ATP depletion and impaired energy metabolism (Bell et al., 2021) or an overactivation of de novo purine synthesis, leading to the accumulation of potentially toxic intermediates of this pathway (López, 2008; López et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about LND pathogenesis supported by citation.

claim: HGPRT deficiency could result from an overactivation of de novo purine synthesis, leading to the accumulation of potentially toxic intermediates.
source: This could result from ATP depletion and impaired energy metabolism (Bell et al., 2021) or an overactivation of de novo purine synthesis, leading to the accumulation of potentially toxic intermediates of this pathway (López, 2008; López et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about LND pathogenesis supported by citations.

claim: Pharmacological models have been developed by injecting the neurotoxin 6-hydroxydopamine into neonatally rat brains, which induced a self-mutilation behavior in response to DA agonist administration in adulthood.
source: Pharmacological models have also been developed by injecting the neurotoxin 6-hydroxydopamine into neonatally rat brains, which induced a self-mutilation behavior in response to DA agonist administration in adulthood. However, these models are of limited utility as they do not reproduce the basic genetic impairment of LND (Breese et al., 1990; Knapp and Breese, 2016; Bell et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about pharmacological models of LND, supported by citations.

claim: Pharmacological models of LND are of limited utility as they do not reproduce the basic genetic impairment of LND.
source: Pharmacological models have also been developed by injecting the neurotoxin 6-hydroxydopamine into neonatally rat brains, which induced a self-mutilation behavior in response to DA agonist administration in adulthood. However, these models are of limited utility as they do not reproduce the basic genetic impairment of LND (Breese et al., 1990; Knapp and Breese, 2016; Bell et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an assessment of the limitations of pharmacological models, supported by citations.

claim: No HGPRT activity has been detected in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: This is probably due to the fact that no HGPRT activity has been detected in this organism (Miller and Collins, 1973; Becker, 1974a; Becker, 1974b).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila purine metabolism, supported by citations.

claim: An ortholog of APRT is expressed in Drosophila, encoded by the Aprt gene.
source: However, an ortholog of APRT is expressed in Drosophila (Johnson et al., 1987), encoded by the Aprt gene.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila genetics, supported by citation.

claim: Part of the functions of human HGPRT, particularly those essential for nervous system development and neurophysiology, may be endorsed by Aprt in Drosophila.
source: It is therefore possible that part of the functions of human HGPRT, and in particular those essential for nervous system development and neurophysiology, are endorsed by Aprt in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on the absence of HGPRT in Drosophila.

claim: Aprt is required during development and in adult stage for many aspects of Drosophila life.
source: We show that Aprt is required during development and in adult stage for many aspects of Drosophila life, and that its activity is of particular importance in subpopulations of brain dopaminergic neurons and glial cells.
evidence: This is supported by various behavioral and molecular assays performed in the study.

claim: Aprt activity is of particular importance in subpopulations of brain dopaminergic neurons and glial cells.
source: We show that Aprt is required during development and in adult stage for many aspects of Drosophila life, and that its activity is of particular importance in subpopulations of brain dopaminergic neurons and glial cells.
evidence: This is supported by cell-specific knockdown experiments showing locomotor defects.

claim: Lack of Aprt appears to decrease adenosinergic signaling.
source: Lack of Aprt appears to decrease adenosinergic signaling and induces both metabolic and neurobehavioral symptoms in flies, as is the case with HGPRT in humans.
evidence: This is supported by measurements of adenosine levels and Ent2 expression.

claim: Lack of Aprt induces both metabolic and neurobehavioral symptoms in flies, as is the case with HGPRT in humans.
source: Lack of Aprt appears to decrease adenosinergic signaling and induces both metabolic and neurobehavioral symptoms in flies, as is the case with HGPRT in humans.
evidence: This is supported by various metabolic and behavioral assays showing similarities between Aprt mutants and LND.

claim: A potential toxic gain-of-function effect of mutated HGPRT had not yet been demonstrated in an animal model.
source: Such a potential toxic gain-of-function effect of mutated HGPRT had not yet been demonstrated in an animal model .
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding regarding mutant HGPRT effects.

claim: All genes related to purine metabolism have homologs in both Drosophila melanogaster and humans, except for the human HPRT1 gene encoding HGPRT and the lack of urate oxidase in humans.
source: The pathways of purine anabolism/catabolism and recycling have been closely conserved between Drosophila melanogaster and humans (Figure 1—figure supplement 1): all genes related to purine metabolism have homologs in both species, except for the human HPRT1 gene encoding HGPRT (step 13 in Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which has no ortholog in flies, and the lack of urate oxidase in humans (step 20).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis and comparison of purine metabolism pathways shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: No HGPRT enzymatic activity can be detected in extracts of wild-type D. melanogaster using either hypoxanthine or guanine as substrate.
source: In accordance with pioneering reports from about 50 years ago (Miller and Collins, 1973; Becker, 1974a; Becker, 1974b), we confirmed that no HGPRT enzymatic activity can be detected in extracts of wild-type D. melanogaster (see below Table 2), using either hypoxanthine or guanine as substrate in the reaction medium.
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic assays shown in Table 2 and confirmed by previous studies.

claim: HGPRT proteins are ancient, present in both bacteria and archaea.
source: HGPRT proteins are ancient, for they are present in both bacteria and archaea.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: HGPRT proteins are strikingly rare in Insecta.
source: However, the analysis of the phyletic distribution of HGPRT proteins revealed their striking rareness in insecta.
evidence: This is supported by PSI-Blast sequence similarity searches on the NCBI Insecta database.

claim: The only 11 HGPRT proteins found in Insecta cluster mainly with bacteria, but also with fungi, apicomplexa, and acari.
source: Phylogenetic analysis showed that the only 11 HGPRT proteins found in Insecta cluster mainly with bacteria, but also with fungi, apicomplexa, and acari (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, red font, see legend for details).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: HGPRT was acquired in a few insecta species by horizontal gene transfer.
source: These and further evidence support the acquisition of HGPRT in a few insecta species by horizontal gene transfer (G. Matassi, unpublished observations).
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic analysis and clustering patterns.

claim: HGPRT has no homolog in Drosophilidae, with the potential exception of Drosophila immigrans.
source: In particular, HGPRT has no homolog in Drosophilidae, with the potential exception of a single species, Drosophila immigrans, in which our most recent PSI-BLAST analysis detected one hit (accession KAH8256851.1, annotated as hypothetical protein).
evidence: This is supported by PSI-BLAST analysis of Drosophilidae genomes.

claim: The D. immigrans HGPRT sequence is 100% identical to the HGPRT of the Gammaproteobacterium Serratia marcescens.
source: Yet this sequence is 100% identical to the HGPRT of the Gammaproteobacterium Serratia marcescens.
evidence: This is supported by sequence comparison analysis.

claim: The D. immigrans HGPRT clusters with the Serratia genus in phylogenetic analysis.
source: A phylogenetic analysis showed that the D. immigrans HGPRT clusters with the Serratia genus (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting either a contamination of the sequenced sample or a very recent horizontal gene transfer event.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The D. immigrans HGPRT likely resulted from a very recent horizontal gene transfer event rather than contamination.
source: The second scenario is more likely since the corresponding nucleotide sequences differ by five synonymous substitutions (out of 534 positions).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of synonymous substitutions in the nucleotide sequence.

claim: Structural similarity searches did not identify any protein with relevant similarity to HGPRT 3D structure in D. melanogaster.
source: We also carried out structural similarity searches against the RCSB Protein Data Bank repository using the human HGPRT structure as query (PDB identifiers: 5HIA or 1Z7G). This analysis did not identify any protein with a divergent sequence and relevant similarity with HGPRT 3D structure in D. melanogaster, consistent with the lack of HGPRT enzymatic activity in this organism.
evidence: This is supported by structural similarity searches against protein databases.

claim: The Aprt5 mutant was originally generated by chemical mutagenesis followed by selection of flies resistant to purine toxicity.
source: The Aprt5 mutant was originally generated by chemical mutagenesis followed by selection of flies resistant to purine toxicity (Johnson and Friedman, 1981; Johnson and Friedman, 1983).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the origin of the Aprt5 mutant, supported by citations.

claim: Enzymatic assays confirmed a strong reduction in Aprt activity in extracts of heterozygous Aprt5/+ mutants and its absence in homozygous and hemizygous mutants.
source: Enzymatic assays confirmed a strong reduction in Aprt activity in extracts of heterozygous Aprt5/+ mutants and its absence in homozygous and hemizygous (Aprt5/Df(3L)ED4284) mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic activity measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and Table 1.

claim: The Aprt5 mRNA codes for a protein with several amino acid changes compared to D. melanogaster wild-type Aprt.
source: Sequencing of the Aprt5 cDNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A) indicated that the Aprt5 mRNA codes for a protein with several amino acid changes compared to D. melanogaster wild-type Aprt, modifying in particular three amino acid residues that have been conserved in the Aprt sequences from Drosophila to humans (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is supported by cDNA sequencing and protein alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The mutations in Aprt5 modify three amino acid residues that have been conserved in the Aprt sequences from Drosophila to humans.
source: Sequencing of the Aprt5 cDNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A) indicated that the Aprt5 mRNA codes for a protein with several amino acid changes compared to D. melanogaster wild-type Aprt, modifying in particular three amino acid residues that have been conserved in the Aprt sequences from Drosophila to humans (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is supported by protein sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: The mutations in Aprt5 are likely to be responsible for the loss of enzymatic activity.
source: These mutations are likely to be responsible for the loss of enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of the mutated residues and the loss of activity.

claim: Homozygous Aprt5 mutants are considered viable because they develop and reproduce normally.
source: The homozygous Aprt5 mutants are considered viable because they develop and reproduce normally.
evidence: This is an observation about the viability of Aprt5 mutants.

claim: Homozygous Aprt5 mutants have a significantly reduced longevity, with a median lifespan of 38 days compared to 50 days for wild-type flies.
source: However, we observed that these mutants have a significantly reduced longevity, their median lifespan being only 38 d against 50 d for wild-type flies (p<0.001) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by longevity assay data shown in Figure 1A.

source: Table 1. Aprt activity in wild-type and Aprt-deficient flies.
evidence: This is directly stated in Table 1.

source: Table 1. Aprt activity in wild-type and Aprt-deficient flies.

source: Table 1. Aprt activity in wild-type and Aprt-deficient flies.

claim: The level of uric acid was substantially increased by 37.7% on average in Drosophila Aprt5 mutant heads.
source: We assayed the levels of purine metabolites by HPLC and found that the level of uric acid was substantially increased by 37.7% on average in Drosophila Aprt5 mutant heads (p<0.01) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Administration of 100 μg/ml allopurinol during 5 days decreased uric acid levels to a normal concentration range in Aprt5 mutant heads.
source: Remarkably, the administration of 100 μg/ml allopurinol during 5 d decreased uric acid levels to a normal concentration range in Aprt5 mutant heads (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The lack of Aprt activity in flies increases uric acid levels and this metabolic disturbance can be prevented by allopurinol, similarly to HGPRT deficit in humans.
source: Therefore, quite similarly to HGPRT deficit in humans, the lack of Aprt activity in flies increases uric acid levels and this metabolic disturbance can be prevented by allopurinol.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and comparison with human LND.

claim: Aprt5 mutant flies showed a very early SING defect starting from 1 day after eclosion (PI = 0.73 vs 0.98 for wild-type flies).
source: Strikingly, Aprt5 mutant flies showed a very early SING defect starting from 1 day after eclosion (d a.E.) (performance index [PI] = 0.73 vs 0.98 for wild-type flies, p<0.001) that was more pronounced at 8 d a.E. (PI = 0.51 vs 0.96 for the wild-type flies, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The SING defect in Aprt5 mutants was more pronounced at 8 days after eclosion (PI = 0.51 vs 0.96 for wild-type flies).
source: Strikingly, Aprt5 mutant flies showed a very early SING defect starting from 1 day after eclosion (d a.E.) (performance index [PI] = 0.73 vs 0.98 for wild-type flies, p<0.001) that was more pronounced at 8 d a.E. (PI = 0.51 vs 0.96 for the wild-type flies, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The fly locomotor performance in Aprt5 mutants did not further decline after 8 days until 30 days after eclosion.
source: The fly locomotor performance did not further decline afterwards until 30 d a.E. (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Hemizygous Aprt5/Df(3L)ED4284 flies displayed SING defects at 10 days after eclosion (PI = 0.71 compared to 0.97 for wild-type flies).
source: Hemizygous Aprt5/Df(3L)ED4284 or Aprt5/Df(3L)BSC365 flies also displayed SING defects at 10 d a.E. (PI = 0.71 and 0.68, respectively, compared to 0.97 for wild-type flies, p<0.01) (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: Hemizygous Aprt5/Df(3L)BSC365 flies displayed SING defects at 10 days after eclosion (PI = 0.68 compared to 0.97 for wild-type flies).
source: Hemizygous Aprt5/Df(3L)ED4284 or Aprt5/Df(3L)BSC365 flies also displayed SING defects at 10 d a.E. (PI = 0.71 and 0.68, respectively, compared to 0.97 for wild-type flies, p<0.01) (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: Allopurinol treatment did not improve the locomotor ability of Aprt5 mutant flies, either administered 5 days before the test or throughout the development.
source: In contrast to its beneficial effect on uric acid levels, we observed that allopurinol treatment did not improve the locomotor ability of Aprt5 mutant flies, either administered 5 d before the test or throughout the development (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: The lack of effect of allopurinol on locomotor ability in Aprt5 mutants is comparable to the lack of effect of this drug against neurological defects in LND patients.
source: This is comparable to the lack of effect of this drug against neurological defects in LND patients.
evidence: This is a comparison drawn between the fly model and human LND.

claim: UAS-AprtRNAi reduced Aprt activity by more than 95% when expressed in all cells with the da-Gal4 driver.
source: To confirm the effect of Aprt deficiency on the SING behavior, we used an UAS-AprtRNAi line that reduced Aprt activity by more than 95% when expressed in all cells with the da-Gal4 driver (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic activity measurements shown in Table 1.

claim: Aprt knock-down flies showed a strong SING defect at 10 days after eclosion (PI = 0.62 against 0.97 and 0.85 for the driver and UAS-AprtRNAi alone controls).
source: These Aprt knock-down flies also showed a strong SING defect at 10 d a.E. (PI = 0.62 against 0.97 and 0.85 for the driver and UAS-AprtRNAi alone controls, respectively, p<0.001), like the Aprt5 mutant (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Tub-Gal80ts; da-Gal4>AprtRNAi flies raised at permissive temperature (18°C) did not show any locomotor impairment.
source: Tub-Gal80ts; da-Gal4>AprtRNAi flies raised at permissive temperature (18°C) did not show any locomotor impairment (Figure 1G, white bars).
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: After being transferred for 3 days at restrictive temperature (30°C), Tub-Gal80ts; da-Gal4>AprtRNAi flies demonstrated a similar SING defect as Aprt5 mutants (PI = 0.63 compared to 0.94 and 0.83 for controls).
source: However, after being transferred for 3 d (between 7 and 10 d a.E.) at a restrictive temperature (30°C) that inactivates Gal80, the same flies demonstrated a similar SING defect as Aprt5 mutants (PI = 0.63 compared to 0.94 and 0.83 for the driver and RNAi alone controls, respectively, p<0.001) (Figure 1G, yellow bars with dots).
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Aprt inactivation at the adult stage only is sufficient to alter SING performance in Drosophila.
source: This demonstrates that Aprt inactivation at the adult stage only is sufficient to alter SING performance in Drosophila, strongly suggesting that this genotype does not result from developmental defects.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal control experiment using Gal80ts.

claim: Expression in all neurons with elav-Gal4 led to decreased locomotor performance in the SING test (PI = 0.68 at 10 days after eclosion, vs 0.90 and 0.86 for controls).
source: Expression in all neurons with elav-Gal4 led to decreased locomotor performance in the SING test (PI = 0.68 at 10 d a.E., vs 0.90 and 0.86 for the driver and RNAi controls, respectively, p<0.05) (Figure 2A), which was comparable to the effects observed with the Aprt5 mutant or after ubiquitous expression of the RNAi.
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Re-expressing Drosophila Aprt selectively in neurons in Aprt5 background partially rescued the SING phenotype (PI = 0.70 vs 0.52 for controls in Aprt5 background).
source: We then found that re-expressing Drosophila Aprt selectively in neurons in Aprt5 background partially rescued the SING phenotype of the null mutant (PI = 0.70 vs 0.52 for driver and UAS-Aprt controls in Aprt5 background, p<0.05) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Aprt knockdown in all glial cells with repo-Gal4 led to a lower SING performance of 10-day-old flies (PI = 0.72 vs 0.91 for both controls).
source: Furthermore, Aprt knockdown in all glial cells with repo-Gal4, or in sub-populations of glial cells that express the glutamate transporter Eaat1 with Eaat1-Gal4, which includes astrocyte-like glia, cortex glia, and some subperineurial glia (Rival et al., 2004; Mazaud et al., 2019), also led to a lower SING performance of 10-day-old flies (PI = 0.72 for repo-Gal4 vs 0.91 for both controls, p<0.05, and PI = 0.56 for Eaat1-Gal4 vs 0.77, p<0.05, and 0.88, p<0.01, for the driver and RNAi controls, respectively) (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Aprt knockdown in glial cells expressing Eaat1 led to a lower SING performance of 10-day-old flies (PI = 0.56 vs 0.77 and 0.88 for controls).
source: Furthermore, Aprt knockdown in all glial cells with repo-Gal4, or in sub-populations of glial cells that express the glutamate transporter Eaat1 with Eaat1-Gal4, which includes astrocyte-like glia, cortex glia, and some subperineurial glia (Rival et al., 2004; Mazaud et al., 2019), also led to a lower SING performance of 10-day-old flies (PI = 0.72 for repo-Gal4 vs 0.91 for both controls, p<0.05, and PI = 0.56 for Eaat1-Gal4 vs 0.77, p<0.05, and 0.88, p<0.01, for the driver and RNAi controls, respectively) (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: MZ0709-Gal4 and NP6520-Gal4 that selectively target the ensheathing glia did not induce any significant locomotor defects when used to express the Aprt RNAi.
source: In contrast, MZ0709-Gal4 (Doherty et al., 2009) and NP6520-Gal4 (Awasaki et al., 2008) that selectively target the ensheathing glia did not induce any significant locomotor defects when used to express the Aprt RNAi (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Re-expressing Aprt with Eaat1-Gal4 in the Aprt5 background did not rescue the SING phenotype.
source: Noticeably, re-expressing Aprt with Eaat1-Gal4 in the Aprt5 background did not rescue the SING phenotype (Figure 2E), in contrast to the positive effect of neuronal re-expression (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Aprt is required both in neurons and glia subsets to ensure a normal SING performance in young flies.
source: Overall this suggests that Aprt is required both in neurons and glia subsets to ensure a normal SING performance in young flies, and that neuronal but not glial Aprt re-expression is sufficient to restore a partially functional locomotor behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell-specific knockdown and rescue experiments.

claim: Neuronal but not glial Aprt re-expression is sufficient to restore a partially functional locomotor behavior.
source: Overall this suggests that Aprt is required both in neurons and glia subsets to ensure a normal SING performance in young flies, and that neuronal but not glial Aprt re-expression is sufficient to restore a partially functional locomotor behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential rescue effects of neuronal vs glial Aprt expression.

claim: Aprt knockdown targeted to DA neurons with TH-Gal4 did not induce significant impairments.
source: Aprt knockdown targeted to these neurons with TH-Gal4 did not induce significant impairments (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: TH-Gal4 expresses in all brain DA neurons except a large part of the PAM cluster.
source: This driver expresses in all brain DA neurons except a large part of the protocerebral anterior medial (PAM) cluster (Friggi-Grelin et al., 2003; Mao and Davis, 2009; Pech et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the expression pattern of TH-Gal4, supported by citations.

claim: Downregulating Aprt with the TH-Gal4, R58E02-Gal4 double driver induced a locomotor defect similar to pan-neuronal Aprt knockdown (PI = 0.72 vs 0.96 and 0.93 for controls).
source: In contrast, downregulating Aprt with the TH-Gal4, R58E02-Gal4 double driver, which labels all DA neurons including the PAM cluster (Sun et al., 2018), induced a quite similar locomotor defect as did pan-neuronal Aprt knockdown (PI = 0.72 vs 0.96 and 0.93 for the driver and RNAi controls, respectively, p<0.001) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: TH-Gal4, R58E02-Gal4 double driver labels all DA neurons including the PAM cluster.
source: In contrast, downregulating Aprt with the TH-Gal4, R58E02-Gal4 double driver, which labels all DA neurons including the PAM cluster (Sun et al., 2018), induced a quite similar locomotor defect as did pan-neuronal Aprt knockdown (PI = 0.72 vs 0.96 and 0.93 for the driver and RNAi controls, respectively, p<0.001) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the expression pattern of the double driver, supported by citation.

claim: Downregulating Aprt in a majority of the serotonergic neurons with TRH-Gal4 did not induce a SING defect.
source: Besides, downregulating Aprt in a majority of the serotonergic neurons with TRH-Gal4 (Cassar et al., 2015) did not induce a SING defect (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Some DA neurons in the PAM cluster are specifically involved in the locomotor impairments induced by Aprt deficiency.
source: These results suggest that some DA neurons in the PAM cluster are specifically involved in the locomotor impairments induced by Aprt deficiency.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of various DA neuron drivers.

claim: Inhibiting DA synthesis in a subset of 15 PAM DA neurons was able to alter markedly SING performance in aging flies.
source: It has been previously shown in our laboratory that inhibiting DA synthesis in a subset of 15 PAM DA neurons cluster was able to alter markedly SING performance in aging flies (Riemensperger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation.

claim: The degeneration or loss of PAM DA neurons is involved in the SING defects observed in several Drosophila models of Parkinson's disease.
source: We and others also reported that the degeneration or loss of PAM DA neurons is involved in the SING defects observed in several Drosophila models of Parkinson's disease (Riemensperger et al., 2013; Bou Dib et al., 2014; Tas et al., 2018; Pütz et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citations.

claim: Expressing AprtRNAi in the PAM cluster with R58E02-Gal4 reproduced the same motor disturbance as pan-neuronal expression (PI = 0.74 vs 0.96 and 0.85 for controls).
source: Here we found that expressing AprtRNAi in the PAM cluster with R58E02-Gal4 reproduced the same motor disturbance as pan-neuronal expression (PI = 0.74 vs 0.96, p<0.001, and 0.85, p<0.05, for the driver and RNAi controls, respectively) (Figure 3D), and this result was confirmed by using two other PAM drivers (NP6510-Gal4 – expressing only in 15 neurons – and R76F05-Gal4) (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Purine recycling deficiency compromises the correct functioning of PAM neurons, leading to a defective startle-induced locomotion.
source: This strongly suggests that purine recycling deficiency compromises the correct functioning of these neurons, leading to a defective startle-induced locomotion.
evidence: This is inferred from the PAM-specific knockdown experiments.

claim: PAM DA neurons innervate the horizontal lobes of the mushroom bodies.
source: Because PAM DA neurons innervate the horizontal lobes of the mushroom bodies (Liu et al., 2012; Riemensperger et al., 2013), and because this structure has been shown to be involved in the control of startle-induced climbing (Riemensperger et al., 2013; Bou Dib et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2018), we also inactivated Aprt in mushroom body neurons with 238Y-Gal4 that strongly expresses in that structure (Aso et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about neuroanatomy, supported by citations.

claim: The mushroom body structure has been shown to be involved in the control of startle-induced climbing.
source: Because PAM DA neurons innervate the horizontal lobes of the mushroom bodies (Liu et al., 2012; Riemensperger et al., 2013), and because this structure has been shown to be involved in the control of startle-induced climbing (Riemensperger et al., 2013; Bou Dib et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2018), we also inactivated Aprt in mushroom body neurons with 238Y-Gal4 that strongly expresses in that structure (Aso et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mushroom body function, supported by citations.

claim: Inactivating Aprt in mushroom body neurons with 238Y-Gal4 induced a locomotor reactivity impairment (PI = 0.70 vs 0.89 for both controls).
source: Interestingly, this driver did induce a locomotor reactivity impairment (PI = 0.70 vs 0.89 for both controls, p<0.01) (Figure 3G), and the same result was observed with VT30559-Gal4, which is a very specific driver for all the mushroom body intrinsic neurons (Plaçais et al., 2017; Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by SING assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Normal expression of the SING behavior depends on Aprt expression in the PAM and mushroom body neurons in Drosophila.
source: Overall, these results show that normal expression of the SING behavior depends on Aprt expression in the PAM and mushroom body neurons in Drosophila.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell-specific knockdown experiments.

claim: Both the mushroom body and subpopulations of PAM DA neurons are known to be regulators of sleep in Drosophila.
source: Both the mushroom body and subpopulations of PAM DA neurons are known to be regulators of sleep in Drosophila (Nall et al., 2016; Artiushin and Sehgal, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about sleep regulation, supported by citations.

claim: Aprt-deficient flies did not have an altered circadian activity profile.
source: Compared to controls, Aprt-deficient flies did not have an altered circadian activity profile (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), nor any difference in total spontaneous locomotor activity during the day, as quantified by the number of infrared beam cuts (events) per 30 min, but they showed a 26.2% increase in total activity during the night (p<0.001) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by activity monitoring data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Aprt-deficient flies showed a 26.2% increase in total activity during the night.
source: Compared to controls, Aprt-deficient flies did not have an altered circadian activity profile (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), nor any difference in total spontaneous locomotor activity during the day, as quantified by the number of infrared beam cuts (events) per 30 min, but they showed a 26.2% increase in total activity during the night (p<0.001) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by activity monitoring data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Aprt5 mutants slept significantly less than wild-type flies both during day and night.
source: We found that Aprt5 mutants slept significantly less than wild-type flies and that it was the case both during day and night (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by sleep monitoring data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Aprt5 mutants showed a reduced walking speed.
source: These mutants indeed showed a reduced walking speed (Figure 4D) and a smaller average sleep bout duration (Figure 4E), indicating a difficulty to maintain sleep.
evidence: This is supported by locomotion speed measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Aprt5 mutants showed a smaller average sleep bout duration, indicating a difficulty to maintain sleep.
source: These mutants indeed showed a reduced walking speed (Figure 4D) and a smaller average sleep bout duration (Figure 4E), indicating a difficulty to maintain sleep.
evidence: This is supported by sleep bout duration measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The reduced speed in Aprt5 mutants does not seem to be caused by a decreased energetic metabolism since ATP levels in head and thorax were not different from wild-type flies.
source: The reduced speed does not seem to be caused by a decreased energetic metabolism since we could not detect different ATP levels in head and thorax of Aprt5 mutants compared to wild-type flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by ATP measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: RNAi-mediated downregulation of Aprt selectively in neurons significantly decreased sleep duration during day and night.
source: Interestingly, RNAi-mediated downregulation of Aprt selectively in neurons (elav>AprtRNAi flies) also significantly decreased sleep duration during day and night (Figure 4F), whereas glial-only expression (repo>AprtRNAi) had no effect (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by sleep monitoring data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Glial-only expression of AprtRNAi had no effect on sleep.
source: Interestingly, RNAi-mediated downregulation of Aprt selectively in neurons (elav>AprtRNAi flies) also significantly decreased sleep duration during day and night (Figure 4F), whereas glial-only expression (repo>AprtRNAi) had no effect (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by sleep monitoring data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Expressing the RNAi in both neurons and glia had similar effects as in neurons alone on sleep.
source: Expressing the RNAi in both neurons and glia (elav; repo>AprtRNAi) had similar effects as in neurons alone (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by sleep monitoring data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Aprt expression is selectively needed in neurons for a normal sleep pattern in Drosophila.
source: Overall, these results suggest that Aprt expression is selectively needed in neurons for a normal sleep pattern in Drosophila.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell-specific knockdown experiments on sleep.

claim: The global TH protein level appeared to be relatively increased by 17.5% in the Aprt5 mutant brain.
source: However, the global TH protein level appeared not to be decreased, but relatively increased by 17.5% in the Aprt5 mutant brain (p<0.01), in particular around the mushroom bodies, a structure that receives dense dopaminergic projections (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by TH immunostaining quantification shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: DA immunostaining revealed a similarly increased level of this neuromodulator in Aprt5 flies, by 17.0% on average in the entire brain.
source: Moreover, DA immunostaining carried out on whole-mount dissected brains revealed a similarly increased level of this neuromodulator in Aprt5 flies, by 17.0% on average in the entire brain (p<0.01), but not specifically in the mushroom bodies or another part of the brain (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is supported by DA immunostaining quantification shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: The transcript levels of DTH1, encoding the TH neuronal isoform in Drosophila, were increased in Aprt5 mutants compared to wild-type flies.
source: We also found that the transcript levels of DTH1, encoding the TH neuronal isoform in Drosophila, were increased in Aprt5 mutants compared to wild-type flies (Figure 5E), and, conversely, decreased when Aprt was overexpressed ubiquitously (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: DTH1 transcript levels decreased when Aprt was overexpressed ubiquitously.
source: We also found that the transcript levels of DTH1, encoding the TH neuronal isoform in Drosophila, were increased in Aprt5 mutants compared to wild-type flies (Figure 5E), and, conversely, decreased when Aprt was overexpressed ubiquitously (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: DTH1 protein levels are increased in Aprt5 compared to controls.
source: Western blot experiments further indicated that DTH1 protein levels are increased in Aprt5 compared to controls (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: Disruption of the purine salvage pathway does not impede DA synthesis and levels in the Drosophila brain, which are instead slightly increased.
source: This indicates that disruption of the purine salvage pathway does not impede DA synthesis and levels in the Drosophila brain, which are instead slightly increased.
evidence: This is inferred from the TH and DA measurements showing increases rather than decreases.

claim: A significant decrease in adenosine level was found either in whole flies (by 61.0% on average) or in heads (by 48.0%) in Aprt5 mutants.
source: Indeed, we found a significant decrease in adenosine level either in whole flies (by 61.0% on average, p<0.01) or in heads (by 48.0%, p<0.05) in Aprt5 mutants (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by UPLC measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Only one seven-transmembrane-domain adenosine receptor, AdoR, is present in Drosophila.
source: Only one seven-transmembrane-domain adenosine receptor, AdoR, is present in Drosophila, which is very similar to mammalian adenosine receptors (Dolezelova et al., 2007; Brody and Cravchik, 2000), and three putative equilibrative nucleoside transporters (Ent1-3) have been identified (Sankar et al., 2002) but only one, Ent2, showed nucleoside transport activity (Machado et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila adenosine receptors, supported by citations.

claim: Three putative equilibrative nucleoside transporters (Ent1-3) have been identified in Drosophila, but only Ent2 showed nucleoside transport activity.
source: Only one seven-transmembrane-domain adenosine receptor, AdoR, is present in Drosophila, which is very similar to mammalian adenosine receptors (Dolezelova et al., 2007; Brody and Cravchik, 2000), and three putative equilibrative nucleoside transporters (Ent1-3) have been identified (Sankar et al., 2002) but only one, Ent2, showed nucleoside transport activity (Machado et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila nucleoside transporters, supported by citations.

claim: Ent2 has been shown to be enriched in the mushroom bodies.
source: Interestingly, Ent2 has been shown to be enriched in the mushroom bodies and its transcript level to be highly elevated in AdoR mutant flies (Knight et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ent2 expression, supported by citation.

claim: Ent2 transcript level is highly elevated in AdoR mutant flies.
source: Interestingly, Ent2 has been shown to be enriched in the mushroom bodies and its transcript level to be highly elevated in AdoR mutant flies (Knight et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ent2 regulation, supported by citation.

claim: In Aprt5 background, a strong increase in Ent2 mRNAs was observed (2.3-fold higher than wild-type flies).
source: In Aprt5 background, we also observed a strong increase in Ent2 mRNAs (2.3-fold higher than wild-type flies, p<0.001), but no noticeable effect on AdoR transcript level (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: No noticeable effect on AdoR transcript level was observed in Aprt5 background.
source: In Aprt5 background, we also observed a strong increase in Ent2 mRNAs (2.3-fold higher than wild-type flies, p<0.001), but no noticeable effect on AdoR transcript level (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The increased expression of Ent2 could correspond to a compensatory response to adenosine shortage in Aprt5 mutants.
source: The increased expression of Ent2 could correspond to a compensatory response to adenosine shortage in Aprt5 mutants.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain the Ent2 upregulation.

claim: AdoR is highly expressed in adult fly heads.
source: The AdoR receptor is highly expressed in adult fly heads and its ectopic overexpression leads to early larval lethality (Dolezelova et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about AdoR expression, supported by citation.

claim: Ectopic overexpression of AdoR leads to early larval lethality.
source: The AdoR receptor is highly expressed in adult fly heads and its ectopic overexpression leads to early larval lethality (Dolezelova et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about AdoR overexpression effects, supported by citation.

claim: A null mutant of AdoR, AdoRKGex, in which the entire coding sequence is deleted, is fully viable.
source: In contrast, a null mutant of this receptor, AdoRKGex, in which the entire coding sequence is deleted, is fully viable (Wu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the AdoR mutant, supported by citation.

claim: Aprt transcripts were decreased by 29.5% on average in AdoRKGex mutant heads.
source: We found that Aprt transcripts were decreased by 29.5% on average (p<0.001) in AdoRKGex mutant heads (Figure 6C, left panel), while Aprt activity was even more decreased by 78.4% (p<0.001) compared to wild-type flies (Figure 6C, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Aprt activity was decreased by 78.4% in AdoRKGex mutants compared to wild-type flies.
source: We found that Aprt transcripts were decreased by 29.5% on average (p<0.001) in AdoRKGex mutant heads (Figure 6C, left panel), while Aprt activity was even more decreased by 78.4% (p<0.001) compared to wild-type flies (Figure 6C, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic activity measurements shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The decrease in Aprt activity in AdoR mutants likely results from the much increased level of adenosine uptake, which would downregulate Aprt activity by a feedback mechanism.
source: This effect likely results from the much increased level of adenosine uptake in the AdoR mutants (Knight et al., 2010), which would downregulate Aprt activity by a feedback mechanism.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain the Aprt downregulation, supported by citation.

claim: Extracellular adenosine levels must be strongly decreased in Aprt mutant flies.
source: Overall, these data indicate that extracellular adenosine levels must be strongly decreased in Aprt mutant flies, both from the general reduction in adenosine levels and the increased expression of the Ent2 transporter.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced adenosine levels and increased Ent2 expression.

claim: AdoR signaling is expected to be significantly reduced in Aprt mutants.
source: Although AdoR expression is not affected, AdoR signaling is therefore expected to be significantly reduced in Aprt mutants.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced extracellular adenosine levels.

claim: Aged Aprt mutants (at 30 days after eclosion) recovered slowly after a strong mechanical stimulation, taking on average 17.3 seconds compared to 2.5 seconds for wild-type flies.
source: We observed that aged Aprt mutants (at 30 d a.E.) recovered slowly after a strong mechanical stimulation applied by vortexing the vial for 10 s at high speed. These flies took on average 17.3 s to recover and get back on their legs compared to 2.5 s for wild-type flies of the same age (p<0.01) (Figure 7A; see also Figure 7—videos 1 and 2 ).
evidence: This is supported by bang sensitivity assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Some Aprt mutant flies appeared more deeply paralyzed as they did not spontaneously recover unless the vial was stirred.
source: Some of the mutant flies appeared more deeply paralyzed as they did not spontaneously recover unless the vial was stirred, so their recovery time could not be scored.
evidence: This is an observation about the severity of the bang sensitivity phenotype.

claim: Hemizygous flies containing the Aprt5 mutation over two partially overlapping genomic deficiencies showed a BS behavior, with an average longer recovery time of 28.9 seconds and 33.2 seconds.
source: Hemizygous flies of the same age containing the Aprt5 mutation over two partially overlapping genomic deficiencies covering Aprt also showed a BS behavior, with an average longer recovery time of 28.9 s and 33.2 s, respectively (p<0.001) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by bang sensitivity assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: RNAi-mediated downregulation of Aprt in all cells led to BS phenotype in adults at 30 days after eclosion.
source: As shown in Figure 7C, da>AprtRNAi flies at 30 d a.E. indeed displayed seizure after mechanical shock, quite similar to that of the Aprt5 mutants (22.7 s recovery time on average compared to 1.55 s and 0.72 s for the driver and RNAi controls, respectively, p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by bang sensitivity assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Inactivating Aprt selectively in neurons, glial cells, or muscles did not induce a BS phenotype.
source: In contrast, inactivating Aprt selectively in neurons (elav-Gal4), glial cells (repo-Gal4), or muscles (24B-Gal4) did not induce a BS phenotype (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by bang sensitivity assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The BS phenotype requires Aprt knockdown in other cells or in several cell types.
source: This suggests that the BS phenotype requires Aprt knockdown in other cells or in several of these cell types.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of BS phenotype with cell-specific knockdown.

claim: Adult-specific Aprt knockdown in all cells with da-Gal4 for 3 days did not trigger a BS behavior.
source: Finally, in contrast to the SING defect, we observed that adult-specific Aprt knockdown in all cells with da-Gal4 for 3 d did not trigger a BS behavior (Figure 7D), indicating that the BS requires a longer downregulation of the gene or might be the consequence of a developmental defect.
evidence: This is supported by bang sensitivity assay data shown in Figure 7D.
